title: CircoTax: a novel circular representation of differentially abundant microbial ranks
content:
Abstract
One of the most relevant applications of NGS-based microbial abundance analysis is the discovery of taxa that appear as differentially represented between ecological niches. In the last years several methods have been proposed to accomplish this task, invariantly reporting the differentially represented taxa at the appropriate taxonomic rank as well as an adjusted p-value and a log2 fold change, representing the confidence on differential call and the amount of variation recorded. This work describes CircoTax, a specialized R ggplot2 plot representing a rank-aware collection of differentially abundant taxa in an intuitive, compact radial form. Specifically, the CircoTax is a circular plot with sectors encoding the taxonomy depth (from phylum to genus) and, departing from the center, a number of radial bars that reach rank-based sectors whose color and transparency are proportional to the log fold change intensity direction and p-value. The visualization of results is graphically appealing and allows to accommodate tens of differentially abundant ranks each with an associated amount of up or down variation so that results are easily intelligible for each differentially represented taxa at a glance. The software is freely available and can be run natively in R or through a dedicated ShinyApp for an interactive usage.

title: Highly Variable Organic Carbon Burial in Thermokarst Lake Sediments on the Qinghai‐Tibet Plateau
content:
Abstract
Thermokarst lakes are dynamic carbon sinks and sources in permafrost landscapes, but their organic carbon (OC) burial remains poorly constrained. We analyzed 210Pb‐dated sediment cores from 12 thermokarst lakes on the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau to quantify sedimentary OC, total nitrogen (TN), C:N stoichiometry, and recent sediment mass accumulation rates (MAR) and OC burial rates (OCBR). Chronology‐dependent comparisons were restricted to sediment intervals with CRS‐derived calendar years of 1900 or later. Across all sediment layers, OC concentrations (1.12–250 g/kg), TN (0.094–26.1 g/kg), and C:N ratios (1.5–188) exhibited pronounced within‐ and among‐lake variability but with no consistent vertical trends shared across lakes. In post‐1900 sediments, MAR (113–21,964 g/m2/yr) and OCBR (6.1–1,167 gC/m2/yr) also showed substantial within‐core and among‐lake variability. Lake‐level median MAR and OCBR varied from 496 to 5,831 g/m2/yr and from 17.8 to 191 gC/m2/yr, respectively. MAR and OCBR were positively related in most lakes, but the slopes differed markedly, suggesting that similar increases in sediment accumulation translated into different increments of OC burial among lakes. Across lakes, median MAR decreased with mean annual precipitation (MAP), whereas median OCBR increased with MAP; no significant relationships were detected with mean annual temperature, elevation, lake area, or lake depth. These results show that recent OC burial cannot be inferred from sediment accumulation alone, but reflects differences in both sediment supply and the OC content of deposited material, with postdepositional preservation representing an additional potential influence.

title: Carbon Processing Domains: Seasonal and Spatial Controls on Dissolved Organic Carbon in a Montane River
content:
Abstract
Lotic biogeochemical structure and function have been studied extensively, but rivers lack a functional classification system for assessing spatiotemporal variability in solute behavior. Dissolved organic carbon (DOC) is a basal resource for aquatic communities, is chemically complex, and has aquatic and terrestrial sources and sinks. DOC is a large carbon reservoir and quantifying its transport and processing contributes to understanding riverine and global carbon dynamics. Introduction of the Nutrient Processing Domain concept provides a framework for comparing spatiotemporal variation in the relative importance of nutrient sources and sinks along rivers. Here, we extended this approach for DOC by defining carbon processing domains (CPDs) using a reach‐scale mass balance based on upstream and downstream DOC concentrations, discharges, and reach areas. We applied the CPD framework along 216 km of a snowmelt‐dominated montane river in the northern Rocky Mountains, USA, using a 3‐year record comprising 656 DOC measurements. CPD classifications revealed distinct baseflow and snowmelt behavior as river segments transitioned among diluter, enhancer, conduit, compiler, and consumer domains. Breakpoint regressions yielded inferred allochthonous DOC (Ctg) estimates of 259 ± 56 μmol L−1 at low flow and 643 ± 128 μmol L−1 at high flow. A mixed‐effects comparison supported a change in slope near the 0.42 m d−1 operational breakpoint but not an abrupt intercept discontinuity; regime‐specific inferred biological DOC consumption (Fbio) values are therefore interpreted as descriptive extrapolated intercepts rather than evidence of an instantaneous biological shift. Together, these results show how DOC transport and processing vary systematically with hydrologic regime.

title: Marine Plug Flow Bioreactors Provide a High‐Throughput Assay of Potential DOC Bioavailability
content:
Abstract
Dissolved organic carbon (DOC) forms the largest reservoir of reduced carbon in the ocean, yet its bioavailability and the microbial processes governing its transformation remain poorly constrained. Traditional seawater batch cultures have been indispensable for measuring bioavailable DOC (BDOC), but their long incubation times and limited throughput constrain comparisons across environmental gradients and treatments. Here, we adapted marine plug flow bioreactors, glass columns packed with inert glass beads colonized by natural microbial assemblages, to provide a high‐throughput operational assay of potential DOC bioavailability. After approximately 6 months of conditioning, single‐column bioreactor assays consistently removed DOC from coastal surface waters, deep seawater, and surface seawater amended with diatom‐derived organic matter within 4–7 hr. Linking bioreactors in series increased cumulative DOC removal although the number of columns contributing additional removal varied among source waters. In paired experiments, terminal bioreactor DOC removal equaled or exceeded that measured at the final sampling point of seawater batch cultures incubated for weeks to months. Bioreactor‐associated microbial communities were enriched in Planctomycetota and Thermoproteota relative to the free‐living communities in batch cultures, reflecting the distinct microbial assemblages supported by the two approaches. Because bioreactors operate under high‐biomass, attached community conditions that differ from the open ocean, their measurements represent internally comparable estimates of potential DOC bioavailability rather than realized in situ utilization. Used alongside seawater batch cultures, marine bioreactors provide a complementary framework for distinguishing potential DOC bioavailability from realized DOC utilization.

title: A Numerical Study of Submesoscale Processes Generated by Mixed Transitional Layer Instability
content:
Abstract
Mixed transitional layer instability (MTI) was proposed as a mechanism to generate deep‐penetrating submesoscale processes (submesoscales) in the upper ocean. This paper conducts a numerical validation of the MTI theory and provides a comprehensive characterization of its evolution and energetics, which is a necessary step toward identifying or parameterizing this mechanism in the real ocean. Specifically, we employ the Regional Ocean Modeling System with a 1‐km horizontal grid to simulate the evolution of a typical mesoscale front in a zonally reentrant channel. We design a 3‐layer model including mixed, transitional, and deep layers and compare its results with those from a realistically continuous model and a 2‐layer model without the transitional layer. Submesoscales occur in all three models due to the development of baroclinic instability. In the 3‐layer model, submesoscales are more energetic, with larger horizontal and vertical scales than those in the 2‐layer model, and these features are consistent with those in the continuous model and with the MTI theory. The difference between the 3‐ and 2‐layer models arises because the MTI occurring in the former can release available potential energy from both the mixed and transitional layers, leading to a larger energy injection scale and deeper influence depth than the mixed layer instability (MLI) in the latter. These differences allow MTI to transport nutrients and other tracers more effectively than MLI, with implications for biogeochemical cycles and air‐sea interaction. Overall, this study establishes a numerical basis for evaluating MTI's role in real ocean submesoscale dynamics.

title: On the Differential Conditioning of Sub‐Antarctic Mode Water and Antarctic Intermediate Water Over Decadal Time Scales
content:
Abstract
We report results from a meridional transect performed along 150°W, 30°S to 60°S in the Southern Ocean (SO). This study aimed to document the rates of conditioning of Subantarctic Mode Water (SAMW) and Antarctic Intermediate Water (AAIW), which are formed during deep mixing events in the austral winter. The water masses are subducted as they flow toward the northern hemisphere. Chloroflourocarbons (CFCs) were sampled along the section in order to estimate the time since atmospheric equilibration of SAMW and AAIW. Combining this information with standing stock information of other biogeochemical variables along isopycnals allowed rates of change of these variables to be deduced. Results demonstrated that temperature and salinity varied with water mass age, possibly reflecting changes in source waters over decadal time scales. Results also showed remineralization rates of nitrate and phosphate in northbound SAMW were faster than remineralization rates in AAIW. In contrast, silicate remineralization rates were faster in AAIW than in SAMW. These trends are expected to affect macronutrient availability, phytoplankton biogeography and productivity in the north Pacific Ocean, especially when the waters are subsequently mixed upwards into the euphotic zone decades later. Vertical mixing of nitrogen‐rich, SAMW into surface waters would support the growth of more non‐silicious algae (such as nannoplankton, coccolithophores and dinoflagellates) whereas more energetic vertical mixing of deeper AAIW into surface waters will encourage the growth of silicious algae like diatoms.

title: Variability of Dissolved Oxygen in the Strait of Georgia: Seasonal, Intraseasonal, and Interannual Changes Based on the SalishSeaCast Model
content:
Abstract
Dissolved oxygen (DO) variability in the Salish Sea is driven by circulation, deep‐water renewal (DWR), and biological activity across multiple timescales. Using an updated version of the SalishSeaCast model, we investigate these drivers of DO in its largest basin, the Strait of Georgia, from 2012 to 2020. The model's refined parameterizations better resolve the near‐bottom DO dynamics. Sediment oxygen demand peaks in spring, consuming up to 50% of surface production, primarily due to organic matter deposition. Seasonal intrusions of dense, oxygen‐rich water from Juan de Fuca and Haro Straits ventilate the Srait of Georgia, elevating deep DO from winter minima (<100 mmol O2 ${\mathrm{O}}_{2}$ m−3 ${\mathrm{m}}^{-3}$) to summer maxima (>120 mmol O2 ${\mathrm{O}}_{2}$ m−3 ${\mathrm{m}}^{-3}$). Advection dominates this renewal, while mixing and organic matter remineralization shape the vertical DO profile. Interannually, years with weak DWR (e.g., 2017) experience 25%–30% greater deep DO drawdown than strong renewal years (e.g., 2020). This result confirms that while the Haro Strait mixing buffer prevents hypoxia, the threshold can still be approached when renewal fails. The 2017 depletion was stagnation‐driven, not production‐driven: weak renewal prolonged residence times, allowing near‐bottom remineralization to deplete DO despite no increase in primary production. These findings provide a three‐dimensional, process‐resolving assessment of how interannual variability in DWR influences hypoxia development in the Strait of Georgia, demonstrating the critical interaction between physical transport and biogeochemical processes for understanding and predicting DO dynamics.

title: Isotopic Insight Into Nitrate Sources and Cycling in Polar Sea Ice
content:
Abstract
Sea ice alters nitrate (NO3−) availability in polar oceans, yet the influence of sea‐ice type on NO3− sources and cycling remains poorly constrained. We analyzed NO3− concentrations and isotopic compositions (δ15N, δ18O, Δ17O) in Antarctic one‐year and Arctic multi‐year sea ice to investigate NO3− sources and transformation processes. Mean NO3− concentrations were substantially higher in Antarctic one‐year sea ice (3.89 ± 17.75 μmol L−1, with the large standard deviation driven by a few bottom‐layer samples with elevated concentrations) than in Arctic multi‐year sea ice (0.50 ± 0.22 μmol L−1). Δ17O‐based source apportionment showed that atmospheric NO3− contributed 37% ± 11.64% in Arctic multi‐year sea ice, compared with 4% ± 2.69% in Antarctic one‐year sea ice. Despite much lower total NO3− concentrations, Arctic multi‐year sea ice exhibited a higher atmospheric NO3− contribution, indicating better preservation of atmospheric NO3−. Non‐atmospheric NO3−, derived from in situ nitrification and/or underlying seawater, accounted for 96% ± 2.69% and 63% ± 11.64% of the NO3− pool in Antarctic and Arctic sea ice, respectively. Isotopic compositions and nutrient concentrations indicate the occurrence of microbial NO3− cycling in both Antarctic one‐year and Arctic multi‐year sea ice, with more pronounced cycling in Antarctic one‐year sea ice. Collectively, these results suggest that sea‐ice type influences NO3− concentrations, sources, and cycling, highlighting the role of sea ice in NO3− availability in polar marine environments. We acknowledge that nitrite (NO2−) in sea‐ice samples could introduce a degree of uncertainty into isotope interpretations; however, given the relatively low NO2−/(NO2− + NO3−) fractions, this uncertainty is unlikely to have affected our main conclusions.

title: Inverse Model Inferred Time Series of Photosynthesis Parameters From Three Decades of Primary Production Measurements
content:
Abstract
Understanding how phytoplankton photosynthetic physiology varies over seasonal to multi‐decadal time scales is important for assessing changes in ocean productivity and its role in the carbon cycle. Here we show that, at the Bermuda Atlantic Time‐series Study and Hawaii Ocean Time‐series stations, photosynthesis parameters exhibit pronounced seasonal and shorter‐term variability but no statistically significant multi‐decadal trends over more than three decades of observations. To investigate these temporal patterns, we use in situ chlorophyll and primary production profiles together with an inverse model to reconstruct long‐term time series of photosynthesis parameters. The two time series stations have surpassed the 30‐year mark, making data collected there suitable for climatological research. A shifted Gaussian is used as a model for the chlorophyll profile and an exactly solvable model of the production profile is used to infer photosynthesis parameters from measured production profiles. The models yielded high coefficients of determination, which enabled the construction of thirty‐year‐long time series of photosynthesis parameters. The seasonal cycle and long‐term changes in the parameters were analyzed. No statistically significant long‐term trends were detected in the estimated photosynthesis parameters, while substantial variability was observed on shorter time scales. The results highlight the importance of accounting for temporal variability in photosynthesis parameters when modeling ocean primary production.

title: Multiwave Interference Characteristics of Semidiurnal Internal Tides in the Northern South China Sea: Perspective of Energetics From Mooring Array Observations
content:
Abstract
Multiwave interference fundamentally shapes the spatial inhomogeneity of internal tides, yet its impact on vertical structure and its modulation by seasons and eddies in the deep ocean remain poorly constrained by direct observations. Using a cross‐shaped mooring array (∼50‐km resolution) deployed in the northern South China Sea from June 2018 to April 2019, this study quantifies the interference dynamics of mode‐1 semidiurnal internal tides (SITs). Observations show that both the horizontal distribution and vertical structure of SIT energy and flux are largely shaped by the superposition of a primary northwestward beam from the Luzon Strait and a secondary southward beam from the continental slope. A refraction‐modified line source model successfully reproduces the observed heterogeneous patterns. Furthermore, the SIT interference field exhibits significant non‐stationarity. The observed ratio of horizontal kinetic energy to available potential energy exhibits opposite seasonal variations between summer and winter, with larger anomalies near the two source regions and smaller anomalies elsewhere. Further analysis reveals that this pattern stems from the combined effect of reversed seasonal circulation and stratification, which drives opposite and spatially inhomogeneous shifts in the interference pattern. Eddy‐induced currents and stratification also drive opposite interference pattern changes in anticyclonic versus cyclonic eddies, but currents overwhelmingly prevail. Consequently, the interference pattern rotates clockwise in anticyclonic eddies and counterclockwise in cyclonic eddies. The observed energy and flux exhibit pronounced responses to the deflection of the interference pattern. These findings highlight that multiwave interference is a dynamically evolving process that spatiotemporally redistributes tidal energy in the deep ocean.

title: Relationships Among MHC Diversity, Parasites and Secondary Sexual Colouration
content:
ABSTRACT
Sexual selection via honest (costly) signals of fitness can generate patterns in immunogenetic diversity at the major histocompatibility complex (MHC). MHC diversity explains variation in immunocompetence—and therefore fitness—thus impacting the ability to generate honest signals. Differences in guppy (Poecilia reticulata) colour patterns can be driven by opposing selection pressures of predation and female mate choice, but the effect of parasitism has received less attention. By studying 21 wild guppy populations in Trinidad, we sought to quantify covariation among parasitic Gyrodactylus spp. infections, male sexual ornamentation (orange and black colouration) and genetic variation at the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) at both individual and population levels. We found population level support for a correlation between MHC diversity and Gyrodactylus prevalence, including an overall association between MHC supertype composition and prevalence. At the individual level, supertype (functional) diversity again emerged as a more informative measure than allelic richness alone. Predation was associated with Gyrodactylus prevalence and orange, but not black, colouration. Notably, some of these relationships differed between the individual and population levels. Further, much of this variation was explained by processes acting at a broader geographic scale within river drainages, which comprise divergent guppy lineages. These findings suggest that evolutionary history and processes such as genetic drift and gene flow contribute substantially to these relationships, but that ecological variation (i.e., predation) interacts with these processes. Our findings indicate that multi‐trait relationships between colour, immunogenetic diversity and infection are best examined within their broader evolutionary and ecological contexts.

title: Brain Transcriptomic Changes Associated With the Socially Regulated Behavioural Specialisation of Ant Queens
content:
ABSTRACT
Insect societies are characterised by a reproductive division of labour between queens that monopolise egg production and workers that perform all non‐reproductive tasks. The queen specialisation in egg laying is typically considered to be constitutive and independent of environmental conditions, but this common assumption was recently challenged by the finding that the presence of workers both induces and maintains the queen specialisation in several species of ants. However, the molecular changes that translate worker presence into queen behavioural specialisation remain unknown. To investigate the transcriptomic basis of the socially regulated specialisation of ant queens, we produced 93 individual brain transcriptomes from queens of the black garden ant Lasius niger that were experimentally maintained in different social environments. Our transcriptomic analyses revealed that 123 genes were differentially expressed between the brains of queens maintained with and without workers. These genes were enriched for processes related to brain energy metabolism and neuronal plasticity and signalling. By investigating the response of selected genes of interest to further manipulations of the social environment, we identified four candidate genes that fully mirrored the queen behavioural changes. Specifically, their expression changes in response to worker presence were reversible and they did not respond to mere cues of the worker presence. These candidate genes included the transcription factor Krüppel‐homologue 1 and other genes in the juvenile hormone and insulin signalling pathways, both known to regulate multiple aspects of division of labour in social insects. By producing a robust, well‐replicated and well‐controlled investigation of the transcriptomic basis of the behavioural specialisation of ant queens, this study provides a better understanding of the emergence and maintenance of reproductive division of labour in insect societies.

title: SpatioCAD: Context-aware graph diffusion model for pinpointing spatially variable genes in heterogeneous tissues
content:
by Hao Wen, Qunlun Shen, Shuqin Zhang

Spatial transcriptomics enables comprehensive characterization of tissue architecture, and the identification of spatially variable genes (SVGs) is a critical step for defining region-specific molecular markers and uncovering spatially regulated mechanisms across diverse biological contexts. However, most existing methods for SVG detection overlook cell density variations, a major confounding factor in complex tissues such as tumors, where heterogeneous cellularity frequently introduces false-positive calls. Here we present SpatioCAD, a computational framework that explicitly decouples genuine spatial expression patterns from confounding effects driven by cellularity. SpatioCAD introduces a graph diffusion model that inherently incorporates cell-density-aware conditions to simulate expression propagation, supporting the identification of SVGs across a broad range of expression levels. Systematic evaluations on simulated datasets demonstrate its superior statistical power and specificity. Applied to breast cancer, lung cancer, and glioma datasets, SpatioCAD identifies functionally diverse SVGs, including low‑abundance transcripts with established roles in tumor progression, while also recapitulates biologically meaningful tissue architecture features. Importantly, SpatioCAD is fast and scalable to large tissues.

title: The promiscuity and degeneracy of ten unique RNA base-pairing rules can determine the success of adaptive RNA evolution
content:
by Leander Goldbach, Nora S. Martin, Andreas Wagner

The topography of fitness landscapes strongly influences the outcome of Darwinian evolution. This topography in turn is determined by the effects of genotypic changes on phenotypes, such as the structure and function of biomolecules like proteins and RNA. Thus, understanding the evolution of biomolecules requires an understanding of the relationship between genotype and phenotype. Here, we study how this relationship is influenced by the fundamental biochemical rules that determine which RNA bases can form base-pairs in RNA secondary structure. To this end, we computationally study the secondary structure genotype-phenotype maps of RNA molecules using all ten possible different such RNA base-pairing rules. We simulate adaptive evolution on fitness landscapes in which an RNA’s fitness is defined by its secondary structure. We find that the base-pairing rules strongly affect how likely an evolving population is to find the global peak of a fitness landscape. The base-pairing rule of most biological RNA molecules (A-U, G-C, G-U) is among the top three most favorable rules for adaptive evolution, in which over 80% of evolving populations find a landscape’s highest fitness peak. Simple characteristics of the genotype-phenotype map, such as the fraction of genotypes that constitute local peaks can help to predict how likely evolving populations are to find a landscape’s global fitness peak. These characteristics can in turn be explained by two elementary properties of base-pairing rules that we call promiscuity and degeneracy.

title: Direction-selective retinal ganglion cells encode motion direction uniformly, despite having discretely distributed cardinal preferences
content:
by Carlo Paris, Félix Hubert, Felix Franke, Olivier Marre, Matthew Chalk, Ulisse Ferrari

On-Off direction-selective retinal ganglion cells (DS RGCs) exhibit broad tuning curves, responding robustly to motion aligned with or near their preferred direction. These cells comprise four major subtypes, each tuned to motion along one of the four cardinal axes: nasal, superior, temporal, or inferior. However, natural stimuli can move in any direction, and it remains unclear whether intermediate directions are encoded less effectively, or whether this cardinal organization nevertheless supports uniform direction encoding. Here, we combined previous electrophysiological recordings of DS cells presented with a moving light bar stimulus with an information-theoretic measure, the Stimulus Specific Information, to estimate the directional sensitivity of small populations of recorded neurons. This analysis revealed that DS RGC populations are uniformly sensitive across all directions of motion. We then asked whether the observed homogeneous sensitivity was a consequence of DS RGCs maximizing the average stimulus information. Simulations with artificially modified tuning curve widths revealed that DS cells prioritize avoiding pronounced drops in sensitivity over maximizing the average transmitted information. This property reduces large deficits in sensitivity for certain directions, thereby limiting potential “blind spots” in the encoding of motion. More generally, our results raise the possibility that maintaining a high minimum sensitivity could be one factor influencing the organization of sensory representations.

title: Traction force microscopy using temporal information
content:
by Kazuko Hamaoka, Kasumi Kusakari, Hirokazu Tanimoto

Traction force microscopy is a simple, non-invasive method that can quantify cellular contact forces at the cell-substrate interface. It solves an inverse problem of determining the force field from measured substrate deformation. Because this problem is ill-posed with a large condition number, it is necessary to suppress the amplification of measurement noise during inversion. Previous studies have employed algorithms such as regularization or filtering that utilize spatial information to discriminate noise and true signals. Here, we propose an alternative approach that utilizes temporal information of the system. This method employs Kalman filter, a simple data assimilation algorithm in time series analysis, to recover the force field. Using numerically generated data, we show that the method is more accurate than standard algorithms including L2-regularization and is effective at filtering out temporal noise. Using experimental data on locomoting cells, we demonstrate that the method can reliably infer time-varying cellular traction forces. We also demonstrate two extensions of the proposed method: incorporation of additional knowledge and direct inference of low-dimensional force characteristics. These practical advantages will motivate the use of proposed framework for analyzing dynamic cell mechanics.

title: LEM-3/ANKLE1 nuclease prevents the formation of abnormal syncytium to safeguard neuronal differentiation
content:
by Siyu Deng, Chaogu Zheng

In animal development, cells exit the cell cycle after a final round of cell division to differentiate into specialized cell types. However, the impact of failed cytokinesis on the fate specification of postmitotic cells, especially neurons, remains poorly understood. We analyzed the Caenorhabditis elegans mutants lacking the midbody-tethered endonuclease LEM-3/ANKLE1, which resolves chromatin bridges during cytokinesis. Using genetic analysis, fluorescence microscopy, and RNA visualization, we found that unresolved DNA bridges lead to the formation of stable intercellular bridges, creating binucleate syncytia between touch receptor neurons and sister cells, which allows thorough cytoplasmic mixing despite independent nuclear transcription. In some cases, the cytoplasmic linkage between sister cells also led to the suppression of neuronal fates and prevention of apoptotic fates. Thus, LEM-3 prevents syncytium formation to ensure proper cellular differentiation.

title: Resistance mutation supply modulates the benefit of CRISPR immunity against virulent phages in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
content:
by Rosanna C. T. Wright, Simon C. Lovell, Anna Richmond, Christian Harrison, Eleri Ashworth, Aras Kadioglu, Joanne L. Fothergill, Ville-Petri Friman, Edze R. Westra, Michael A. Brockhurst

Only a fraction of bacterial genomes encode CRISPR-Cas systems, but the selective causes of this variation are unexplained. How naturally virulent bacteriophages (phages) select for CRISPR immunity has rarely been tested experimentally. Here, we show against a panel of genetically and functionally diverse virulent phages that CRISPR immunity was not universally beneficial to Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and its fitness effect varied strongly between phages in predictable ways. In addition to mechanisms known to alter the effectiveness of CRISPR immunity, such as encoding a matching spacer or a protective nuclear shell, we show that the fitness effect of CRISPR immunity negatively associated with the probability of evolving receptor-based resistance to the phage via spontaneous mutation. The supply of resistance mutations differed strongly between very closely related lipopolysaccharide-binding phages and was associated with variation at the C-terminus of the tail fibre protein altering residues involved in hydrogen bonding and the predicted binding site. Our results show that CRISPR immunity is more beneficial against virulent phages that are harder to evolve resistance to via receptor mutations, suggesting that virulent phage community composition and diversity will be important drivers of the prevalence of CRISPR immunity.

title: CFL1-dependency of discrete cell behaviours driving mouse spinal zippering
content:
by Abigail R. Marshall, Andrea Krstevski, Henry Crosswell, Rahul Shah, Eirini Maniou, Nicholas D. E. Greene, Andrew J. Copp, Gabriel L. Galea

Epithelial fusion is critical for formation of many embryonic tissues. The developing mammalian spinal cord fuses by zippering, through cell behaviours dependent on F-actin turnover. We propose a caudal-to-rostral sequence of surface ectoderm cell behaviours which drive zippering progression in mice, and test the requirement for the F-actin severing protein CFL1 in this process. Key zipper-advancing behaviours are: (i) constriction of supracellular actomyosin cables; (ii) extension of filopodial/lamellipodial protrusions at periodic intervals; (iii) constriction of leading-edge cell borders bringing together protrusions which establish ‘pioneering’ contacts across the midline; (iv) cell-cell and v. cell-ECM adhesion remodelling; (vi) zipper advancement through cell partner exchange. In wild-type embryos, CFL1 is enriched at the leading edge of surface ectoderm cells adjacent to the zippering point and localised within some protrusions. Conditional Cfl1 deletion in the surface ectoderm produces denser F-actin stress fibres, makes filopodial protrusions excessively stable, diminishes their exploratory movements which may establish nascent contacts, and impairs junctional constriction of cells at the point of fusion. Zippering speed is reduced ~30% in conditional Cfl1-deleted embryos and ~30% develop spina bifida. We therefore propose that impaired filopodial dynamicity and junctional constriction limits the sequence of behaviours driving spinal zippering, predisposing to spina bifida.

title: Fungal suppression by bacterial metabolite-activated human intestinal γδT-cells is disrupted in Crohn’s disease
content:
by Liya Mathew, Sean L. Carlson, Michael Savage, Claire Pardieu, Megan B. O’Brien, Ellie Crawley, Paul Harrow, Ann-Kristin Kaune, Edward Devlin, Emily L. Priest, Marilena Crescente, Kimberly Martinod, James Boot, SoFong Cam Ngan, Marco Gasparetto, Klaartje Kok, James O. Lindsay, Jonathan P. Richardson, Julian R. Naglik, Andrew J. Stagg, Matthias Eberl, Siu Kwan Sze, Carol A. Munro, Neil E. McCarthy

Gut symbionts condition mucosal immunity to resist infection by enteropathogens, but the specific microbes and mechanisms involved differ significantly between host species. In higher primates, bacterial metabolite HMB-PP is sensed by a specialized population of Vγ9Vδ2+T-cells, which we now report can potently suppress growth of endogenous fungi in human intestinal organ cultures. In healthy intestine, HMB-PP-stimulated Vδ2+ T-cells restricted outgrowth of keystone fungus Candida albicans via a mechanism that required IL-22. In Crohn’s disease (CD), Vδ2+ T-cells were poorly responsive to HMB-PP and permitted outgrowth of C. albicans strains that formed toxin-producing filaments, triggered neutrophil extracellular traps, and induced macrophage IL-1β release ex vivo. Genomic and proteomic analysis of the Candida isolates suggested increased tissue adhesion of CD-derived strains, which rapidly invaded the gut barrier in an ‘intestine-on-a-chip’ model. These data reveal that bacterial activation of Vδ2+ T-cells suppresses fungal pathobionts in human gut via an IL-22-dependent mechanism that is dysregulated in CD.

title: Emotion knowledge is structured in a grid-like coordinate system in the human ventromedial prefrontal cortex
content:
by Yumeng Ma, Philip A. Kragel

Human emotional experiences vary widely in everyday life, yet they are systematically organized within a continuous affective space defined by valence and arousal. Although this circumplex organization has shaped decades of research, its neural implementation remains unclear. Here, we asked whether abstract emotion concepts are encoded using grid-like coordinate principles in the human brain. During fMRI, participants tracked trajectories through affective space conveyed through morphs of facial expressions and sequences of phrases. We found that ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) encoded affective space with robust hexadirectional modulation characteristic of grid-like coding. This coordinate representation generalized across stimulus modalities, indicating abstraction beyond perceptual features. The grid-like signal reflected a metric organization of emotion concepts independent of overt behavior, whereas distance-related signals in vmPFC predicted trial-by-trial affective judgements. Together, these findings suggest that emotion knowledge is structured by a grid-like coordinate system in the human brain that can support predictive inference and flexible decision-making.

title: Behavioural and neurogenetic evidence for emotion primitives in the fruit fly Drosophila from an open field test
content: Emotions are based on evolutionarily conserved building blocks (‘emotion primitives’) that are present across mammals. Whether these building blocks are found in insects is largely undefined. Here, we employ the open field test (OFT) in Drosophila and focus on wall-following and total walking activity as behavioural indicators of emotion-like states. Wildtype and transgenic flies were subjected to various conditions prior to behavioural testing. The results indicate that wall-following and total walking activity are independent measures that are modulated, with generally increased wall-following observed under aversive stimuli and decreased values under positive conditions, independent of the time of day. The effects of genetic manipulation of selected neuromodulatory systems support their role in modulating emotion-like states in Drosophila. Activation of reward-related neurons decreased wall-following while inhibition increased it. Moreover, treatment with ethanol or diazepam produced predictable changes in behaviour. Our findings suggest that Drosophila shares conserved core emotion-like building blocks with vertebrates, and show that wall-following and total walking activity in the OFT can serve as a reliable indicator of emotional valence and arousal in the fruit fly. This positions Drosophila as a powerful genetic model to dissect the neuronal and neurochemical substrates of emotion primitives.

title: Reevaluating Large‐Scale Deformation Precursors of Great Subduction Earthquakes: Insights From Satellite Gravity and GNSS Data
content:
Abstract
Validating the controversial hypothesis that precursory gravity changes arise from sudden acceleration of subducting plates potentially triggering great earthquakes is of paramount importance. To rigorously evaluate proposed precursors for the 2011 Mw 9.0 Tohoku and 2010 Mw 8.8 Maule earthquakes, we develop a statistical framework that enables (a) robust assessment of their statistical significance, (b) characterization of temporal evolution, and (c) integrative analysis across multiple GRACE gravity solutions with differing error characteristics. Additionally, we test the precursor hypothesis using independent GNSS‐measured surface displacements within a physically consistent framework. Our results show no evidence supporting the proposed precursor in either alternative GRACE solutions or high‐precision GNSS observations. The anomalous gravity changes previously interpreted as earthquake precursors are indistinguishable from solution‐specific data errors or other non‐tectonic signals, lacking evidence for tectonic origin.

title: Urbanization Enhances Inner‐Core Rainfall During Tropical Cyclone Landfall
content:
Abstract
How urbanization modulates precipitation in landfalling tropical cyclones (LTCs) remains poorly understood. Previous studies disagree on whether the mechanism is primarily dynamical or thermodynamic, particularly within the inner core under intense wind–rain conditions. Using high‐resolution simulations and storm‐relative framework, we quantified the effects of urban land‐cover change (ULCC) and anthropogenic heat (AH) on peak inner‐core precipitation during Typhoon Bebinca's 2024 landfall in Shanghai. Results showed that ULCC induced surface roughness weakened near‐surface tangential winds while strengthening radial inflow and low‐level convergence, increasing precipitation by 13.8% relative to the cropland scenario. Over cropland, AH alone increased precipitation by 19.7% relative to the non‐AH scenario, whereas in the presence of urban surface, AH enhanced thermodynamic instability and deep convection, increasing precipitation by 29.8%, demonstrating that AH enhances rainfall independently of urban surfaces, while ULCC further enhances this response. In other words, urbanization enhances extreme LTC rainfall through thermal–dynamic effects and their coupling.

title: Model‐Data Comparison of Electron Energization Associated With Kinetic Alfvén Waves in the Near Earth Magnetotail
content:
Abstract
A model‐data comparison between Gyrofluid‐Kinetic Electron simulations and MMS satellite observations of kinetic Alfvén waves (KAW) and associated electron energization in the near Earth magnetotail is presented. The observations reveal 10 keV electron beams embedded within intense KAW field‐aligned currents. When constrained by observed plasma and wave parameters, simulations reproduce consistent electron signatures, establishing, for the first time, a direct link between KAWs and the production of these highly energized electrons. Most of the wave Poynting flux gets transferred to the electrons well in advance of the undriven KAW perturbation's arrival at the simulation low‐altitude boundary. Particle tracings reveal that the energized electrons are able to exit out of the simulation low‐altitude boundary and thus can significantly contribute to ionospheric electron precipitation that drive auroral emissions and ionospheric ion outflow.

title: Evaluation‐Constrained Projections Reveal a Potentially Navigable Arctic by the 2030s
content:
Abstract
The rapid decline in Arctic sea ice thickness (SIT) is reshaping Arctic navigation prospects. However, large uncertainties in climate model skill hinder robust projections of future navigability. Here we evaluate SIT simulated by the CMIP6 using satellite, airborne, reanalysis, and in situ data sets across freezing and melting seasons. To better constrain projections, we develop two evaluation‐based model selection schemes. We introduce the climatological concept of a potentially navigable Arctic (PNA), defined as a state in which more than 80% of the Arctic Ocean north of 60°N exhibits SIT below 0.15 m, making most of the Arctic Ocean potentially navigable for vessels with no ice class. Compared to conventional multi‐model mean, evaluation‐based schemes project thinner SIT and earlier navigability. Under both SSP2‐4.5 and SSP5‐8.5 scenarios, PNA conditions are projected to occur in the 2030s, with the number of navigable months reaching four and six by the end of the century, respectively.

title: High Resolution Focal Mechanisms and Stress Field Orientation in Southern Italy From Short‐Term Dense Arrays
content:
Abstract
Understanding fault geometry and mechanics is key to interpreting the seismotectonic setting of a region. We analyze data from a 1‐year dense seismic array deployment in Southern Italy to infer focal mechanisms and stress field from low‐magnitude earthquakes using machine‐learning techniques. We derive 289 focal mechanisms, including nearly all events with ML>1.3 ${M}_{L} > 1.3$, yielding a data set comparable to that obtained from 6 years of conventional monitoring. The retrieved mechanisms are consistent with the orientation of the main tectonic structures, and the stress field, inverted from the principal fault planes, indicates a dominant normal faulting regime. We illustrate that dense monitoring enables investigation of spatio‐temporal characteristics of the stress field, showing homogeneity at ∼20 km spatial scale and temporal stability of principal stress orientations. Furthermore, seasonal variations in the stress ratio are observed, that could be modulated by hydrological loading.

title: Experimental Evidence of Reaction‐Driven Fracturing and Ultramafic Rock Weakening Induced by CO2 Mineralization
content:
Abstract
Carbon sequestration in mafic and ultramafic rocks offers a pathway to mitigate CO2 ${\text{CO}}_{2}$ emissions, while mineralization could precondition rocks for critical mineral extraction. However, the reaction‐driven fracturing processes that increase permeability and weaken rock remain underexplored. Here, we expose serpentinized dunite samples to CO2 ${\text{CO}}_{2}$‐rich Mg(OH)2‐brine at 90°C and 3.5 MPa for up to 32 days, using X‐ray computed tomography and digital volume correlation to quantify morphological evolution and 3D solid displacements. Results reveal tensile microfractures nucleating within 11 days, progressing to core disaggregation, with localized damage concentrated along pre‐existing veins and flaw tips. Calculated crystallization pressures exceeding 100 MPa, together with fracture mechanics modeling, support magnesite formation within brucite‐filled veins as the primary driver for reaction‐driven fracturing. Raman spectroscopy and scanning electron microscopy help identify mineral changes. These insights into spatiotemporal dynamics of reaction‐driven fracturing can inform strategies for CO2 ${\text{CO}}_{2}$ injection and mineralization in ultramafic formations.

title: Enhanced Sensitivity of the Asian Water Tower to La Niña in the 21st Century
content:
Abstract
The Tibetan Plateau (TP) is a key water source for downstream Asia, and its rainy‐season precipitation is influenced by the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO). However, whether this teleconnection has remained stationary over recent decades remains uncertain. Using multi‐source data sets, we examine ENSO‐related precipitation, circulation, and moisture‐transport composites during the pre‐2000 epoch (1979–2000) and the post‐2001 epoch (2001–2023). ENSO lifecycle composites show that El Niño and La Niña are associated with opposite‐signed precipitation responses through changes in Western Pacific Subtropical High (WPSH) displacement and monsoon moisture transport. In the post‐2001 epoch, the sensitivity of the plateau's rainy‐season precipitation to La Niña is enhanced: La Niña‐related wetting and WPSH responses are larger in the composites, with a more westward‐displaced WPSH and enhanced moisture transport toward the plateau.

title: How the River Network Shapes Spatiotemporal Drought Behavior Across Europe
content:
Abstract
Understanding spatial drought relationships is important for effective drought relief. The river network—that is, the system of rivers, channels, lakes, and reservoirs within a river basin—influences spatial streamflow drought connectivity and modulates drought characteristics. However, these effects are difficult to disentangle from spatial drought dependencies originating from other hydro‐meteorological processes. Here, we use high‐resolution hydrological model simulations over Europe and study the river network effect in isolation by comparing drought extents of unrouted runoff to those of routed discharge. We find that the river network increases drought extent in most European basins. Runoff droughts in snowmelt‐dominated upstream regions often lead to larger discharge droughts than the original runoff drought, whereas discharge droughts in downstream rivers are affected by runoff droughts upstream. Water bodies influence the river network effect by storing water, thereby decoupling runoff from discharge. Our results can help water managers to better understand spatiotemporal drought development.

title: Spatial patterns in phytoplankton community composition and their relationship to carbon export on the northwest Weddell Sea continental shelf
content:
Spatial patterns in phytoplankton community composition and their relationship to carbon export on the northwest Weddell Sea continental shelf
Meredith G. Meyer, Robert J. W. Brewin, Xuerong Sun, Clara Manno, Florence Atherden, Sasha J. Kramer, Giorgio Dall'Olmo, and Karen J. Heywood
